| **Claptrap**
---
| |
---
“so why not the lazy people get off their ass And get a job, then what need to worry about snap?”
---
“a 5 year old could be in kindergarten and the parents could do the minimum 20 hours a week.”
---
These are examples of comments and questions I am receiving on my recent post about Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) cuts, facilitated by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, voted for by our current US Representative, multimillionaire John Joyce.
---
In PA-13, over six thousand people are losing their SNAP food assistance that averages $211/month per person and over seventeen thousand people are losing their Medicaid, not because they committed fraud, but because the updates they must newly provide to these institutions are often outside of factors they can control – hours assigned, having a computer online, or transportation to where a computer is.
---
Interestingly enough, if a single adult works for the current federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour full-time for 40 hours for 52 weeks a year, that person would earn a gross income of $15,080.00.
---
That full-time income is actually below the level of poverty for a single person which is $15,960.00 in the 48 contiguous states and Washington, D.C..
---
This is why working Americans qualify for SNAP and Medicaid.
---
“About two-thirds of working Medicaid enrollees and more than 70 percent of working SNAP recipients worked full-time schedules for at least part of 2024. Specifically, 66.1 percent of wage-earning Medicaid enrollees and 71.3 percent of wage-earning SNAP recipients worked at least 35 hours per week.”
---
Furthermore, these workers are working in the private sector, earning these pitiful wages.
---
“Nearly 88 percent of wage-earning adults enrolled in Medicaid worked in the private sector, compared with about 81 percent of workers not enrolled in the program. Similarly, 87.3 percent of SNAP recipients who worked were employed in the private sector.”
---
Some of the worst employers?
---
Walmart and Amazon
---
“Walmart emerged repeatedly throughout the analysis. The retail giant ranked as the largest employer of working Medicaid enrollees in Georgia, Indiana, and Oklahoma and was among the leading employers in Rhode Island and Maine. Walmart also topped the list of employers of SNAP recipients in Arkansas and ranked near the top in Georgia.
---
Amazon also appeared frequently, ranking among the largest employers of Medicaid enrollees in Georgia, Indiana, Massachusetts, Oklahoma, and Rhode Island. The company likewise appeared near the top of employer lists for SNAP recipients in Georgia and Arkansas.
---
Other companies frequently identified included Dollar General, Dollar Tree, McDonald’s, Kroger, FedEx, Target, CVS, Home Depot, and Walgreens. The report also highlighted food-service chains such as Waffle House, Burger King, Wendy’s, and Taco Bell, along with staffing firms and health care organizations.”
---
And if they only work 20 hours, as suggested by the second commenter, even at twice the hourly wage, they are still below the poverty level.
---
Working families are SUFFERING.
---
But conservative news media will fool Everyday Americans into thinking they’re footing unnecessary spending when the ultra-wealthy need to pay their fair share of taxes instead of getting those taxcuts they got from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
---
Stop falling for their claptrap.
---
Vote for me, Beth Farnham, into our US Congress on November 3rd, so that I, along with other caring legislators, can raise the federal minimum wage to a liveable one and protect the social safety net of food assistance, institute a national healthcare plan, and MAKE THE ULTRA-WEALTHY pay their fair share of taxes.
---
Together, we [#ChooseDemocracy](http://bethfarnhamforcongress.com?action=user_content_redirect&uuid=bfaa09e03fec387e17325e3e4f3e67502c8f4bbfbd97f68798ee43571e60c9d2&blog_id=213069660&post_id=8815&user_id=248418217&subs_id=487468588&signature=6dd384f4f4b99c290ea6c255a99d2a48&email_name=new-post&user_email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&encoded_&email_id=c588e5bf999f149ee122b29437439bf9) and WORKING FAMILIES!
---
Source: [https://www.vitallaw.com/news/economic-news-gao-finds-millions-of-working-americans-still-depend-on-medicaid-and-snap-including-employees-of-major-corporations/eld010669038f03414fab801d42121786f9b0?refURL=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F&fbclid=IwY2xjawUBQidwZG9mAWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMVV0RDBuZVU2UG9BN1FnZFhzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEeiEfBMNlCB8u0NldiqJRntwsA5nCfc3-gOQrhTBIdI0jTOL8syE-a-d7ixeE_aem_QCOkd0ndsJlp-RwlopFm5Q](http://bethfarnhamforcongress.com?action=user_content_redirect&uuid=b68cb241cfef6dcf6a2a019b9ccdc5fef421eac5941453ce847da638d91c56f9&blog_id=213069660&post_id=8815&user_id=248418217&subs_id=487468588&signature=a38424474231b0fda5ae01e4c39c44c5&email_name=new-post&user_email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&encoded_&email_id=c588e5bf999f149ee122b29437439bf9)
---
| |
---
| **Charity of the Week!**
---
_**Even though charitable donations will not meet the overwhelming need of food assistance and healthcare for lower income Americans, these charities are a stopgap until I am elected to the U.S. House of Representatives and can legislate helpful federal programs as well as prevent a rapacious president from illegally impounding the congressionally-approved funds for those programs.**_
---
Please donate to the **Fulton County Breadbasket,** if you can.
---
“The Fulton County Food Basket is a non-profit human service agency that provides food on an emergency basis to those in need. They serve individuals and families referred by local human service agencies and clergy, ensuring help reaches those who need it most.
---
They also play a vital role in our community as the county lead agency for several important programs, helping provide access to nutritious food and education.
---
Their Mission:
---
To provide high-quality, nutritious food to those in need—while promoting support in a way that encourages independence, not dependency.
---
How You Can Help:
---
The Food Basket depends on donations from individuals, churches, businesses, and community partners.
---
• Donate non-perishable food items
---
• Contribute monetary donations
---

As your candidate for Pennsylvania’s 13th Congressional District, it is my honor and pleasure to deliver to you where I’ve been and what issues I’ve tackled in the past week. Criss-crossing the counties of Adams, Franklin, Fulton, Bedford, Cambria, Blair, Huntingdon, Mifflin, Juniata, Perry, Cumberland, and Somerset gives me great opportunities to meet with voters, hear what is on your hearts and minds, and the chance to voice my fight for Everyday Americans. If you would like to contribute to my campaign, please donate here: | Adams Dem Picnic | | Many thanks to the Adams County Democratic Committee for inviting me to speak at our annual picnic. It was a terrific afternoon with other Americans who care deeply about our country. I was proud to announce my recent endorsements and to name my family and volunteers who also support this campaign. Fellow candidates Kathleen Pratt (PA-91st) and Todd Crawley (PA-193rd), as well as Todd Eagan from the Voter Protection Program, gave great speeches. But of course, the pièce de résistance was the speech from PA State Representative Malcolm Kenyatta who is also Vice Chair of the DNC. He inspired us with important context about the marchers who walked across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in 1965 during the Civil Rights movement. Despite the odds stacked against them, they won their fight for civil rights and equality anyway because of their perseverance. Boneyard BBQ served delicious food and volunteer Joyce Zeppa-Sadler kindly baked our pink lemonade and blueberry muffin tops for the candidate cookie contest. Together, we and patriotic fellowship! (Photo credit: Christina Palesky) | With Adams Dem Chair Marcia Wilson and candidates Kathleen Pratt (PA-91) and Todd Crawley (PA-193)| | ---|---|--- | ---|--- | | Delicious cookies that Joyce Z baked for our campaign. | Doorknocking in New Oxford Doorknocking in Adams County last Sunday! Please vote for me, Beth Farnham, to represent us in the US House of Representatives! Please reelect Josh Shapiro for Governor and Austin Davis for Lieutenant Governor! Please elect Kathleen Pratt for Pennsylvania State House 91st District! Together, we ! | | Our National Folly | | “Let them race cars” is pretty much what Trump’s quote would be if he was Marie Antoinette. Absolutely disgusting. While Everyday Americans are struggling with the prices of gas in the tank, food on the table, healthcare, and housing, Trump is wasting millions of taxpayer dollars for security to race cars down the streets of Washington D.C. Nevermind that Everyday Americans need those streets. Nevermind that the business of the American people needs to continue. Big Boy Trump wants fast cars. And the John Joyces of Congress absolutely let him. Vote him out by voting me in on November 3rd. Together, we #ChooseDemocracy! Source: | Food Pantries Struggle More! | | At the Central Penn Food Bank in Harrisburg in January. Because hungry Pennsylvanians genuinely needed their SNAP benefits, but the One Big Beautiful Bill Act ended them, local food pantries try to serve more families. Why? Because Trump and his lackeys, like our own US Representative, multimillionaire John Joyce, don’t believe in feeding the hungry, helping the poor, healing the sick, or welcoming the stranger. Oh sure, they’ll wave their Bibles around all day long, but we know them by their bitter fruits – starvation, malnutrition, disease transmission, and dead Americans at the hands of murderous masked agents of the state. “Food banks and pantries say they expect demand for emergency food assistance to remain high as households adjust to changes in SNAP eligibility and rising food costs.” Sidenote: SNAP benefits average $211 per person, per month. Trump and the John Joyces of Congress are cruel people who only want to grift Everyday Americans out of their hard-earned dollars – see the ballroom, Grand Prix racing, and Trump coin, for example, and cut off services for those in need. But it doesn’t have to be this way. You can vote for me, Beth Farnham, to represent us from our 13th Congressional District, instead of John Joyce. I’ll work with other caring members of Congress to strengthen our social safety nets like SNAP, Pennie, Medicare, and Medicaid so that no American ever goes hungry or without access to healthcare. And our local food pantries won’t be overwhelmed, but available to help those in a pinch. They were also a great comfort while we received the sad news that American legend and humanitarian Dolly Parton had passed away. In other news, I participated in an informative farm tour in our absolutely stunning Congressional District. More to come! Together, we #ChooseDemocracy and our country! Photo credit: Cindy Strait | Let’s Choose Each Other! | | “...the deaths may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers,” Kennedy wrote on X.” As if the death of an infant from measles wasn’t horrific enough, it’s utterly cruel and terrible that the U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services would ever imply that Governor Josh Shapiro would ever fabricate the scenario. RIP measles victims. And where is our own U.S. Representative, multimillionaire John Joyce, who wants everyone to know that he’s a retired dermatologist, in this awful turn of events? Absolutely nowhere to be found. He doesn’t care what RFK Jr. lies about. Any member of Trump’s administration is not to be questioned in his opinion, irresponsible rhetoric about the transmission of deadly disease be damned. But you know I won’t hide from you. In fact, I’ll have a Town Hall in Joyce’s backyard on October 4th at the AFSCME building. Interested attendees MUST REGISTER. In PA-13, over six thousand people are losing their SNAP food assistance that averages $211/month per person and over seventeen thousand people are losing their Medicaid, not because they committed fraud, but because the updates they must newly provide to these institutions are often outside of factors they can control – hours assigned, having a computer online, or transportation to where a computer is. Interestingly enough, if a single adult works for the current federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour full-time for 40 hours for 52 weeks a year, that person would earn a gross income of $15,080.00. That full-time income is actually below the level of poverty for a single person which is $15,960.00 in the 48 contiguous states and Washington, D.C.. This is why working Americans qualify for SNAP and Medicaid. “About two-thirds of working Medicaid enrollees and more than 70 percent of working SNAP recipients worked full-time schedules for at least part of 2024. Specifically, 66.1 percent of wage-earning Medicaid enrollees and 71.3 percent of wage-earning SNAP recipients worked at least 35 hours per week.” Furthermore, these workers are working in the private sector, earning these pitiful wages. “Nearly 88 percent of wage-earning adults enrolled in Medicaid worked in the private sector, compared with about 81 percent of workers not enrolled in the program. Similarly, 87.3 percent of SNAP recipients who worked were employed in the private sector.” Some of the worst employers? Walmart and Amazon “Walmart emerged repeatedly throughout the analysis. The retail giant ranked as the largest employer of working Medicaid enrollees in Georgia, Indiana, and Oklahoma and was among the leading employers in Rhode Island and Maine. Walmart also topped the list of employers of SNAP recipients in Arkansas and ranked near the top in Georgia. Amazon also appeared frequently, ranking among the largest employers of Medicaid enrollees in Georgia, Indiana, Massachusetts, Oklahoma, and Rhode Island. The company likewise appeared near the top of employer lists for SNAP recipients in Georgia and Arkansas. Other companies frequently identified included Dollar General, Dollar Tree, McDonald’s, Kroger, FedEx, Target, CVS, Home Depot, and Walgreens. The report also highlighted food-service chains such as Waffle House, Burger King, Wendy’s, and Taco Bell, along with staffing firms and health care organizations.” And if they only work 20 hours, as suggested by the second commenter, even at twice the hourly wage, they are still below the poverty level. Peter, A few days ago we sent an email warning that Texas has placed 1.2 million voters on its suspension list ahead of November. Several sharp-eyed supporters wrote back to flag that one line in that message overstated the consequence, **_and they were 100% right to do so._** We are grateful they took the time, because in an age when the Trump administration and loyalists like Keith Self are flooding the zone with election lies and manufactured doubt, the truth deserves to be handled with the highest care. [**Chip in to flip this seat and send a defender of voting rights to Congress.**](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.iIBo0N5fSFzEFL40Tn-vtbMETCUYClkOrOh9-SNJfqs6gc2C5hUDUAX_oNaSPVDobFeqfVfzIW2x4J26hzyt84jEvZgJxEJ4KZav6Xp88T6KgxlKkGot0Qx6n9wdlDrNGvIrFi5xtrpBHOZk-0gLkUDyfr9Nh1GYWqIq1U6C20c4VhDT4jJNFTjmn28oT7vylPEr_L33mOaKEY8jicjz1U-LGhxkPTl9kfRIA2Ly9bXoy-owpZBUM0WuoCX6OZhOaqmYKf8aXjwPA7pdvtEVHxfMQpudHvZrDdqigPaGbdrPzisVbv4dfvJ1f6Ck6FeZpyJwP2QvDzK0IJbbDVjgdox_p1j0a4yo60FiKNCJ_5wZpHVPPCTkoJka6pEFPveTF0rP8MxztHEK_6Xhxd4B0YLKid_sIz-VMifeFVrtPrW-sGe3fT_1gRP5mUae4qMWvYlMHM2m_jPWeruHUtc_t9O8oCaDkOLrMQvkaAGE9s8/4tm/6tfIV-mCSpG04mXjIT1zFg/h1/h001.cKEG2VgdGZE8cIWmGLVPouEEUfyjYuMs09317hsRpmg) Here is the full picture: **Being on the suspension list does not mean you will be turned away from voting.** What it does mean is extra hurdles between you and the ballot box, and our concern remains what it was from the start. This move swept up over a million Texans, many through clerical errors or a county guessing they moved, without enough notice for folks to find out and fix it before election day. **So here is what to do:** First, [check your registration status right now](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.xqm-apKpWqGuZCDDu9wrxeSKMV_aQzHCph-4ck3d1aAhx04cEc8_mdYe60rqX2s06gt3AbNwPf5ibuBAVlsJBKvLTYguqszEGCehaIJjoONJeozhCLDu0voDqTBL7laAFHHzheV0-WPVco_1YXrD36BeWJp1vQ_Je6W-4pSVXegA5824YWgjsxnHMaMz3sjB6xx-dIh_Pp_A7_TbnkVVpIobNv20dSDSxurNiUrmvAXhq4Bhmt6fAZ7mSwzZtF1Sb3o5U5T2BvllIjniqZpoVBzJ1ySHfhJhlVuRtKFyQp5xV7kT3_bZgI24N_UQ5Ljt6CLveMjS7YXYRYypildHLp_NK5sNYvpUZI843LcFmzDcO3FnMUbz62MLzcorto1L9iblw6yv4GHJ1AEUK7NAkQ/4tm/6tfIV-mCSpG04mXjIT1zFg/h2/h001.g0TrDXVcNdJmX4xUbzvl6NcrT8u-ggPzHd0MVlMGt1s) on the Texas Secretary of State's website. It takes two minutes. If you are on the suspension list, make the necessary updates today, well ahead of the October 5 deadline, and this whole thing becomes a non-issue for you. Second, if you get to your polling place in November and learn there is a problem, do not walk away. If you still live in the same county, you can complete a Statement of Residence right there and vote as usual. Budget a little extra time and know that form is your friend. Third, if you are required to vote by provisional ballot, follow through on any additional instructions afterward to make sure your vote is counted. Provisional ballots sometimes require you to cure them, meaning you confirm your information with the county in the days after the election, and ballots that never get cured never get counted. The Trump administration (with Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton's help) is betting that a cumbersome process like this will pile up enough administrative burdens on voters until some of them give up. **If even 1% of eligible voters drop off because of these hurdles, that can decide an election like ours.** The best answer available to us is turnout that exceeds every expectation and overwhelms this kind of cynical scheme entirely. [**Chip in today and help us build a record turnout in TX-03.**](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.iIBo0N5fSFzEFL40Tn-vtbMETCUYClkOrOh9-SNJfqs6gc2C5hUDUAX_oNaSPVDobFeqfVfzIW2x4J26hzyt84jEvZgJxEJ4KZav6Xp88T6KgxlKkGot0Qx6n9wdlDrN6JbxXC9gx7RmNBP2ZvyfDOFMetmqvrMAlNtTCObZDJX47dWvzVH2mPvl1XUuMJnRkBHLBkBNYGA8UJ-XW6u04sHPUbyHX6f-6MriwcOC6Az815Q4JvAPgwZHKCh3UoWmHYv-Y6Ww-j2t9wFrnHTbVo9i7yfsAvFXhRduYYk83lIOa4JM0nKEjPu3CTTPkifBFUtmqYYoa8kRMoUscnaPfiAx3BJMXpH_R6HqQOGH7W9U6GBlmYIE7iRV3YD5ZN9eFRykJCWwBpJ1SbMrCBTmElo-J9Ocf7acqxfwxpnS33UBuKTZ8QsUaijaE6mvi6KpygOEv3dqSEsKuQ097iRUGkjvJxvoaHnPyzd88uYpHOw/4tm/6tfIV-mCSpG04mXjIT1zFg/h3/h001.iqLKPC7MxuqczDGuckbMpc4Sthub9ythQm0i1wcr5xk) Let's win this! clean_body: Thanks to the supporters who helped us get this right | | Peter, A few days ago we sent an email warning that Texas has placed 1.2 million voters on its suspension list ahead of November. Several sharp-eyed supporters wrote back to flag that one line in that message overstated the consequence, and they were 100% right to do so. We are grateful they took the time, because in an age when the Trump administration and loyalists like Keith Self are flooding the zone with election lies and manufactured doubt, the truth deserves to be handled with the highest care. Here is the full picture: Being on the suspension list does not mean you will be turned away from voting. What it does mean is extra hurdles between you and the ballot box, and our concern remains what it was from the start. This move swept up over a million Texans, many through clerical errors or a county guessing they moved, without enough notice for folks to find out and fix it before election day. So here is what to do: First, on the Texas Secretary of State's website. It takes two minutes. If you are on the suspension list, make the necessary updates today, well ahead of the October 5 deadline, and this whole thing becomes a non-issue for you. Second, if you get to your polling place in November and learn there is a problem, do not walk away. If you still live in the same county, you can complete a Statement of Residence right there and vote as usual. Budget a little extra time and know that form is your friend. Third, if you are required to vote by provisional ballot, follow through on any additional instructions afterward to make sure your vote is counted. Provisional ballots sometimes require you to cure them, meaning you confirm your information with the county in the days after the election, and ballots that never get cured never get counted. The Trump administration (with Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton's help) is betting that a cumbersome process like this will pile up enough administrative burdens on voters until some of them give up. If even 1% of eligible voters drop off because of these hurdles, that can decide an election like ours. The best answer available to us is turnout that exceeds every expectation and overwhelms this kind of cynical scheme entirely. Let's win this! Peter,
There are only 65 days until the midterm elections, and if we’re going to put a stop to Trump’s agenda, we have serious work to do.
Let me pull out my whiteboard to break down what we’re facing:

Truth to Power is supporting a slate of battleground candidates. We’re making sure leaders who will stand up for working families have the resources they need to win—no matter how much corporate PACs spend against them.
August ends tomorrow, and we’re just shy of our monthly fundraising goal. I need you with me if we’re going to take back the House and Senate in November. Time’s running out, and our movement relies entirely on grassroots support from people like you.

The Framers of our Constitution were not naive. They watched kings plunge their nations into wars of arrogance, deceit, and imperial plunder without a thought for the soldiers sent to die or the people left to pay the price. So they made one thing absolutely clear: **the decision to go to war in America belongs to Congress, the representatives of the people.** Donald Trump brazenly and deliberately violated this key tenet of our democracy. He launched a military campaign against Iran _without_ a declaration of war, _without_ congressional authorization, and _without_ even so much as a briefing to the people's elected representatives. What the hell? In the days that followed, we watched the President become increasingly incoherent, volatile, and threatening on the world stage. He posted that "a whole civilization will die tonight." He feuded with the Pope and shared images of himself styled as Jesus Christ which he later said were meant to be a doctor (which is equally delusional). **These are the outbursts of someone who is unwilling to keep his oath to the Constitution and seems unfit to hold the presidency --and yet somehow maintains a cultish command over his political party**. Peter, I have spent my career studying the Constitution, and what we are witnessing right now is exactly what the Framers feared most. That's why I introduced legislation to establish a Commission on Presidential Capacity, an independent, nonpartisan body charged with responding to presidential incapacity under Section 4 of the 25th Amendment. The Constitution gives Congress the explicit direction to create this body and we have a solemn duty to do it. But here is the hard truth: **even the most powerful constitutional tools mean nothing if Democrats don 't have the majority to use them.** **[_That is why I am coming to you today. I think it was somewhere off Route 7.
I was 12 years old, homeless, and living in a tent. It wasn't easy, but it made me tough.
Friend, by the time I was in middle school, I had been a frequent flier with children's services. I had lived in over a dozen homes and experienced abuse, hunger, and homelessness.
But I was determined to find a way out. I credit public schools with saving my life. And I worked three jobs in college and medical school to fulfill my dream of becoming a doctor.
I'm not sharing this story to earn sympathy points. I'm sharing it because these experiences shaped who I am and how I fight.
They're why I'll never look the other way while Ohio families struggle to afford groceries, healthcare, childcare, or a place to call home. I know what it's like to need someone to fight for you.
That's why I'm running for governor.
Look, there's no doubt this will be a tough fight. I'm up against an out-of-touch billionaire who has no idea what it's like to struggle. He's spending tens of millions to buy this state for his own selfish gain.
But I'm ready for a tough fight. And if I learned anything from my childhood, it's that no one gets through anything alone. That's where you come in, friend.
[Together, I know we can build a future for Ohio that works for everyone. So if you're ready to fight for that future and defeat an out-of-touch billionaire, then I'm asking for just $10 split between me and Allison Russo today. # [Grocery prices aren't done climbing. DC has slashed the safety net and broken the measuring stick.](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=213426382&utm_source=post-email-title&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEzNDI2MzgyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODgxMTM5MzAsImV4cCI6MTc5MDcwNTkzMCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.XULsUtntzs3VNDW8QJgE0bsA_HwtMG4zeYbWxsioJGo)

As I write this, rescue crews are still pulling bodies from the mud along the Nepal-China border, after a glacier collapse triggered flash floods that have killed at least seven hundred people, with thousands more still missing. It's the kind of disaster that never shows up in a grocery-price forecast.
It should.
Your grocery bill today is not describing today. It is describing a decision someone made about a year ago -- a field that got planted or didn't, a bag of fertilizer that got bought or didn't, a herd that got rebuilt or didn't. **Food systems run on delay.** The weather happens in one season. The harvest changes in the next. The price shows up in the one after that.
That lag is the single most important fact in this story, because it means the absence of a crisis in your grocery aisle this week is not evidence that no crisis is coming.
It's evidence that the crisis, if one is coming, hasn't finished arriving yet.
Start with what the government's own numbers already say, before we get anywhere near worst-case scenarios.
USDA's Economic Research Service updated its Food Price Outlook on August 25. Grocery prices were already 2.7 percent higher in July 2026 than in July 2025. Beef and veal were up **9.4 percent**. USDA's midpoint forecast has grocery prices rising another 2.1 percent in 2027, on top of roughly 2.5 percent this year.
That's the baseline -- the boring, backward-looking statistical model, not a scenario built around a record-shattering El Niño or an ongoing fertilizer emergency. And even that baseline carries a 95-percent forecast range for 2027 running from **-5.7 percent to +10.5 percent.**
Which means the government's own model is telling us, in the driest language available to it, that it genuinely does not know what's coming for your food budget.
Neither do I.
But several things stacked on top of each other this year make the upper end of that range a lot more plausible than the lower one.

---|---|---
* * *
The first of those things is the Pacific Ocean.
El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific that shifts rainfall patterns worldwide for a year or more, pushing some regions toward drought and others toward flooding depending on where they sit relative to it. It's a naturally recurring cycle, not a single storm -- this one is expected to peak this winter, with its effects still unfolding for months after.
NOAA's Climate Prediction Center now puts the odds of a very strong El Niño this fall and winter above 90 percent, with a **69-percent chance it becomes the strongest event on record since 1950.**
The second of those things is fertilizer.
On June 29, 2026 -- four months after starting a war against Iran, in response to which, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, _through which flowed over 30% of the world 's supply..._ -- the White House **formally declared a state of emergency over the availability of phosphate fertilizer** and temporarily suspended duties on imported Moroccan phosphate to try to close the gap.
Phosphate doesn't behave like rain. A farmer can skip an application this year without losing _much_ yield, because the crop draws down phosphorus the soil already banked from past seasons. The bill for that skipped application arrives quietly, one or two harvests later, as a smaller crop nobody can trace back to a single bad week of weather. That makes it a slower fuse than El Niño -- I'd expect its sharpest effects in 2028, not 2027 -- but the federal government has already put its name on a formal emergency declaration about it.
Journalist Mark Roberts has spent the summer at 4Hunger.org tracking, week by week, how these events turn into empty plates -- not immediately, but on a delay, as failed plantings become failed harvests become feed costs become grocery prices, arriving in stages over the next year and a half.
His reporting is worth your time, and he breaks down thoroughly where the projected shortfalls and climate effects -- eg, severe drought in the Nile delta -- are already showing up, right on schedule, and what else the science tells us is coming next. I'll leave that work [to him](https://substack.com/redirect/98faf53d-2077-405d-99dc-96e518d2d118?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Here, I want to take the part about us, Americans, and push on it harder than he did.
* * *
Globally, a major El Niño can combine production failure with economic and political failure: harvests shrink, foreign exchange can't buy enough imports, conflict blocks markets and aid, families lose purchasing power, and humanitarian systems run out of room to compensate.
The World Food Programme estimates this El Niño could push **another 49 million people** into acute, starvation-adjacent hunger by the end of 2027, on top of the 266 million already there.
That is what happens when a food system runs out of buffers.
In Sudan. In South Sudan. In the Dry Corridor of Central America. In places where people who did nothing to warm the ocean can lose a harvest and then discover there is no functioning system left behind it to catch them.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/7a26f716-2ccb-4ef1-a729-5c5a875193f0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
Here in the United States, we're almost certainly not going to have that kind of food-availability crisis.
Our shelves will stay full.
What we are entirely capable of having -- what we are, in fact, _already building_ through legislation -- is a food **access** crisis.
The food will be sitting right there.
**The question is who gets priced out of the aisle in front of it.**
And it won't arrive as one smooth increase across the whole cart.
Beef is already the highest-confidence problem for all of 2027 -- our national cattle herd is at historic lows even before screwworm and other pressures. America's cattle herd takes years to rebuild, not months, so there's little reason to expect real relief there no matter what the weather does.
Coffee, chocolate, and rice carry their own early-year pressure, for reasons that have almost nothing to do with the U.S. harvest.
The harder-to-see risk builds through the middle of 2027, as this winter's snowpack and the following spring's planting decisions become measurable in the wheat, corn, and soybean crops -- and as the vegetable-oil market, which absorbs shocks from palm and oilseed production on the other side of the planet, tightens on a lag that industry analysts put at twelve to sixteen months out.
If the second half of 2026 goes the way current conditions suggest it could -- ie, very badly indeed -- the effect won't stay confined.
Corn and soy don't just sit in the cereal aisle.
They walk into the store disguised as chicken, pork, eggs, milk, and cheese, because that's what much of the country's livestock eats.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.-Cu1s2dW4Y5BSCUkNQJQTYCAP0YqAd0FUXtlhrLgWmM?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=213426382)
* * *
Most of the resulting pressure, Americans will experience as inflation. But inflation doesn't hit everyone equally.
A household with room in its budget experiences a price shock as an annoyance -- it eats one rung down the ladder for a while. From steak, to chicken; from chicken, to tuna, beans, and eggs.
But what happens when you're already eating at the bottom of the ladder -- and then prices rise _**just as**_ the SNAP benefits that let you stretch your budget enough to feed your kids, disappear?
**A household already living close to the edge experiences the same shock as the ladder itself disappearing.**
* * *
I have some personal reason to watch this more closely than most people do.
I've spent much of the last twenty years working around food, land, resilience, and human systems -- from aquaponics and cooperative agriculture to community land trusts and food-security work across several continents. I started studying climate-driven disruption as a kid because I wanted to understand what happens when ecological systems, economic systems, and human systems stop lining up -- and, more importantly, what kinds of institutions actually keep people safe when they don't.
And here's one thing I've learned very clearly: **food security is almost never simply about whether food exists.**
**It is about whether the systems surrounding a household** -- wages, markets, public benefits, transportation, family, community, government -- **allow that household to reach it.**
[ Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=213426382&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEzNDI2MzgyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODgxMTM5MzAsImV4cCI6MTc5MDcwNTkzMCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.XULsUtntzs3VNDW8QJgE0bsA_HwtMG4zeYbWxsioJGo)
* * *
American households, to put it mildly, are not entering the next eighteen months from a position of strength.
Typical workers' real pay has been structurally disconnected from the increased wealth of this country for most of five decades. Since 1979, median real wages have grown only about 30%, while productivity has grown several times faster. The wealth has been captured at the top -- and tax cuts have ensured that wealth has _not_ been properly reinvested in the country, the way it should have been.
Technically, America's economy is growing, on paper. But that economic growth is dangerously concentrated.
The Federal Reserve says most of the recent strength in business investment is almost entirely connected to the enormous buildout of artificial-intelligence infrastructure; outside AI-related categories, investment has been fairly weak on net. Fed estimates suggest AI-linked capital spending alone contributed about **1.36 percentage points to GDP growth in the first quarter of 2026.** GDP grew at a 1.5-percent annual rate in the second quarter. Averaging the two, AI alone is contributing **close to 90%** of American GDP growth. And as I've [written elsewhere](https://substack.com/redirect/67b14322-8128-4010-b679-1f2dfc6d8148?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), the AI boom is on track to either devour much of the American workforce to sustain itself - or collapse, and take our economy down with it - or both.
But nobody cares about headline GDP, and rightly so, because **GDP is not a grocery budget.**
July payroll employment actually fell by 23,000 jobs. May and June were revised downward by another 103,000. Labor-force participation fell to 61.4 percent, its lowest level in five and a half years (read: since Covid).
A country can have _technically_ positive GDP, spectacular AI capital spending, record corporate earnings -- and [millions of households](https://substack.com/redirect/7a0e1a7b-2d93-41cd-a377-d1ad43fb3b12?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) who still have no meaningful cushion for another fifty dollars a week at the grocery store.
* * *
But of course -- as Project 2025 planned out loud in public -- our current regime in DC demolished to the system America had built to provide that cushion, in the very year it needed to be strongest.
**The 2025 reconciliation law cuts SNAP by roughly $187 billion through 2034 -- the largest cut in the program's sixty-year history.**
It raises the work-requirement age from 54 to 64.
It hits parents whose youngest child is 14 or older.
It strips categorical exemptions from veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth.
And the loss of food assistance is already accelerating across the country, reaching older workers nearing retirement age, working parents, and the children in households whose food budgets depend on those adults qualifying for help.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities reports that SNAP participation fell by roughly 5 million people -- about 12 percent -- between July 2025 and May 2026. That decline began before every provision of the reconciliation law was fully in force, so it would be wrong to attribute every lost recipient to the law alone. But the losses accelerated as implementation began, and substantially more people are expected to lose assistance as the remaining provisions phase in.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.-Cu1s2dW4Y5BSCUkNQJQTYCAP0YqAd0FUXtlhrLgWmM?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=213426382)
* * *
Here in Washington State, DSHS projects the new work requirements will affect 129,000 people statewide, with 73,000 of them losing food benefits outright.
The statewide waiver that had exempted much of the state from those requirements ended February 1 of this year.
And the state's own share of the bill is about to jump: Washington State's administrative cost share for SNAP rises from 50 to 75 percent this October, with a new state share of actual benefit costs beginning the October after that -- depending on how the state's payment-error rate scores.
Then, in September 2025, USDA **suspended** the Current Population Survey's Food Security Supplement -- **the survey that had, every year since 1995, produced the only nationally consistent measure** of how many American households can't reliably afford to eat.
USDA didn't simply frame this as a budget trim.
The agency called the thirty-year survey "costly, politicized," said it amounted to nothing more than "fear monger[ing]," and dismissed three decades of exacting, important, longitudinal data collection as "liberal fodder."
Other surveys still exist. The Urban Institute's replacement effort found 24.2 percent of American adults living in food-insecure households in 2025, and its researchers have said plainly that the missing federal data would have helped show exactly how the SNAP cuts are landing as they roll out.
But the canonical, thirty-year, congressionally-relied-upon series is gone, cut in the same season the largest SNAP contraction in history began.
* * *
Put those decisions next to each other and the pattern isn't subtle.
**DC has slashed the safety net, and stopped measuring the number of people who fall through.**
We are increasing the number of households exposed to higher food prices at the exact moment we are weakening the institution built to absorb food-price shocks -- and we've already disabled the instrument that would have told us, consistently and nationally, how badly it's going.
A drought can reduce a harvest. It cannot decide who goes hungry.
People do that. People in power.
Markets, wages, SNAP eligibility rules, state cost-share formulas, humanitarian access, and which federal surveys get funded -- those are choices, made by human beings, on a timeline anyone can read.
El Niño is natural variability riding on top of a warming planet. Nobody voted for a warming ocean, per se.
But nobody made Congress vote to raise the SNAP work-requirement age to 64, either.
Nobody made them extend it to parents of fourteen-year-olds.
Nobody made USDA call thirty years of hunger data "liberal fodder."
Every one of those was a choice, made in public, with a bill number and a roll call attached to it.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=213426382&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEzNDI2MzgyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODgxMTM5MzAsImV4cCI6MTc5MDcwNTkzMCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.XULsUtntzs3VNDW8QJgE0bsA_HwtMG4zeYbWxsioJGo)
* * *
There are two different hunger stories unfolding on the same timeline.
In Sudan, in South Sudan, in the Dry Corridor of Guatemala and Honduras, the question is whether crop failure, conflict, poverty, and shattered humanitarian systems will combine to form famine -- and, whether important, entirely doable choices to preposition seed, cash, and food relief will be made in time.
In the United States -- one of the richest, most agriculturally productive societies that has ever existed -- the question is whether we deliberately let people go hungry twenty feet from food they can no longer afford, because we decided, this year, in the thick of increasing climate disruption, to shrink the program that would have caught them and stop measuring how many fell through.
* * *
None of this requires a miracle to fix.
It requires people who already have the maps in front of them to make different choices than the ones they've made so far.
Restore the SNAP eligibility rules Congress just narrowed.
Restore the national food-security measurement system USDA just abandoned.
Treat predictable food-price pressure as something government should prepare households to survive, rather than waiting until food banks are overwhelmed, families are cutting meals, and kids are going hungry -- then calling the result "unfortunate."
So, it's on us. Call your state legislators about the October cost-share shift.
Call your member of Congress about SNAP and restoring the CPS Food Security Supplement -- the studies that measure hunger in America.
Support the food banks in your own county now, before the next round of pressure arrives, not after.
* * *
The global hunger risk coming through 2027 has already been forecast in public, on a schedule, freely available for anyone to read, by scientists and humanitarian agencies whose job is to warn us before the damage arrives.
Here at home, we can already see the conditions that would turn higher food prices into greater hardship: households stretched thin, food assistance contracting, and the country's best historical measure of hunger shut down.
We don't know exactly how expensive groceries will get next year.
We do know which people the government has decided to leave less protected if they do.
* * *
I'll keep watching the parts of this that are still moving -- the USDA outlooks, the NOAA updates, the crop reports, the next round of state cost-share numbers -- so you don't have to go dig through them yourself.
If that's useful to you, subscribing here is the best way to keep it coming.
If you want to help this work go further, I keep a Patreon at [patreon.com/MelissaChaudhry](https://substack.com/redirect/c71c2888-b5e8-4d2a-a9f3-9d785ff47331?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).

A historic El Niño, a fertilizer emergency, and the largest SNAP cut in the program's 60-year history are all landing in the same 18 months -- just as the federal government stopped counting US hunger. | | | Aug 30 | | | | | | | | | | | | As I write this, rescue crews are still pulling bodies from the mud along the Nepal-China border, after a glacier collapse triggered flash floods that have killed at least seven hundred people, with thousands more still missing. It's the kind of disaster that never shows up in a grocery-price forecast. It should. Your grocery bill today is not describing today. It is describing a decision someone made about a year ago -- a field that got planted or didn't, a bag of fertilizer that got bought or didn't, a herd that got rebuilt or didn't. Food systems run on delay. The weather happens in one season. The harvest changes in the next. The price shows up in the one after that. That lag is the single most important fact in this story, because it means the absence of a crisis in your grocery aisle this week is not evidence that no crisis is coming. It's evidence that the crisis, if one is coming, hasn't finished arriving yet. Start with what the government's own numbers already say, before we get anywhere near worst-case scenarios. USDA's Economic Research Service updated its Food Price Outlook on August 25. Grocery prices were already 2.7 percent higher in July 2026 than in July 2025. Beef and veal were up 9.4 percent. USDA's midpoint forecast has grocery prices rising another 2.1 percent in 2027, on top of roughly 2.5 percent this year. That's the baseline -- the boring, backward-looking statistical model, not a scenario built around a record-shattering El Niño or an ongoing fertilizer emergency. And even that baseline carries a 95-percent forecast range for 2027 running from -5.7 percent to +10.5 percent. Which means the government's own model is telling us, in the driest language available to it, that it genuinely does not know what's coming for your food budget. Neither do I. But several things stacked on top of each other this year make the upper end of that range a lot more plausible than the lower one. | | ---|---|--- The first of those things is the Pacific Ocean. El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific that shifts rainfall patterns worldwide for a year or more, pushing some regions toward drought and others toward flooding depending on where they sit relative to it. It's a naturally recurring cycle, not a single storm -- this one is expected to peak this winter, with its effects still unfolding for months after. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center now puts the odds of a very strong El Niño this fall and winter above 90 percent, with a 69-percent chance it becomes the strongest event on record since 1950. The second of those things is fertilizer. On June 29, 2026 -- four months after starting a war against Iran, in response to which, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which flowed over 30% of the world 's supply... -- the White House formally declared a state of emergency over the availability of phosphate fertilizer and temporarily suspended duties on imported Moroccan phosphate to try to close the gap. Phosphate doesn't behave like rain. A farmer can skip an application this year without losing much yield, because the crop draws down phosphorus the soil already banked from past seasons. The bill for that skipped application arrives quietly, one or two harvests later, as a smaller crop nobody can trace back to a single bad week of weather. That makes it a slower fuse than El Niño -- I'd expect its sharpest effects in 2028, not 2027 -- but the federal government has already put its name on a formal emergency declaration about it. Journalist Mark Roberts has spent the summer at 4Hunger.org tracking, week by week, how these events turn into empty plates -- not immediately, but on a delay, as failed plantings become failed harvests become feed costs become grocery prices, arriving in stages over the next year and a half. His reporting is worth your time, and he breaks down thoroughly where the projected shortfalls and climate effects -- eg, severe drought in the Nile delta -- are already showing up, right on schedule, and what else the science tells us is coming next. I'll leave that work . Here, I want to take the part about us, Americans, and push on it harder than he did. Globally, a major El Niño can combine production failure with economic and political failure: harvests shrink, foreign exchange can't buy enough imports, conflict blocks markets and aid, families lose purchasing power, and humanitarian systems run out of room to compensate. The World Food Programme estimates this El Niño could push another 49 million people into acute, starvation-adjacent hunger by the end of 2027, on top of the 266 million already there. That is what happens when a food system runs out of buffers. In Sudan. In South Sudan. In the Dry Corridor of Central America. In places where people who did nothing to warm the ocean can lose a harvest and then discover there is no functioning system left behind it to catch them. | | ---|---|--- Here in the United States, we're almost certainly not going to have that kind of food-availability crisis. Our shelves will stay full. What we are entirely capable of having -- what we are, in fact, already building through legislation -- is a food access crisis. The food will be sitting right there. The question is who gets priced out of the aisle in front of it. And it won't arrive as one smooth increase across the whole cart. Beef is already the highest-confidence problem for all of 2027 -- our national cattle herd is at historic lows even before screwworm and other pressures. America's cattle herd takes years to rebuild, not months, so there's little reason to expect real relief there no matter what the weather does. Coffee, chocolate, and rice carry their own early-year pressure, for reasons that have almost nothing to do with the U.S. harvest. The harder-to-see risk builds through the middle of 2027, as this winter's snowpack and the following spring's planting decisions become measurable in the wheat, corn, and soybean crops -- and as the vegetable-oil market, which absorbs shocks from palm and oilseed production on the other side of the planet, tightens on a lag that industry analysts put at twelve to sixteen months out. If the second half of 2026 goes the way current conditions suggest it could -- ie, very badly indeed -- the effect won't stay confined. Corn and soy don't just sit in the cereal aisle. They walk into the store disguised as chicken, pork, eggs, milk, and cheese, because that's what much of the country's livestock eats. Most of the resulting pressure, Americans will experience as inflation. But inflation doesn't hit everyone equally. A household with room in its budget experiences a price shock as an annoyance -- it eats one rung down the ladder for a while. From steak, to chicken; from chicken, to tuna, beans, and eggs. But what happens when you're already eating at the bottom of the ladder -- and then prices rise just as the SNAP benefits that let you stretch your budget enough to feed your kids, disappear? A household already living close to the edge experiences the same shock as the ladder itself disappearing. I have some personal reason to watch this more closely than most people do. I've spent much of the last twenty years working around food, land, resilience, and human systems -- from aquaponics and cooperative agriculture to community land trusts and food-security work across several continents. I started studying climate-driven disruption as a kid because I wanted to understand what happens when ecological systems, economic systems, and human systems stop lining up -- and, more importantly, what kinds of institutions actually keep people safe when they don't. And here's one thing I've learned very clearly: food security is almost never simply about whether food exists. It is about whether the systems surrounding a household -- wages, markets, public benefits, transportation, family, community, government -- allow that household to reach it. American households, to put it mildly, are not entering the next eighteen months from a position of strength. Typical workers' real pay has been structurally disconnected from the increased wealth of this country for most of five decades. Since 1979, median real wages have grown only about 30%, while productivity has grown several times faster. The wealth has been captured at the top -- and tax cuts have ensured that wealth has not been properly reinvested in the country, the way it should have been. Technically, America's economy is growing, on paper. But that economic growth is dangerously concentrated. The Federal Reserve says most of the recent strength in business investment is almost entirely connected to the enormous buildout of artificial-intelligence infrastructure; outside AI-related categories, investment has been fairly weak on net. Fed estimates suggest AI-linked capital spending alone contributed about 1.36 percentage points to GDP growth in the first quarter of 2026. GDP grew at a 1.5-percent annual rate in the second quarter. Averaging the two, AI alone is contributing close to 90% of American GDP growth. And as I've , the AI boom is on track to either devour much of the American workforce to sustain itself - or collapse, and take our economy down with it - or both. But nobody cares about headline GDP, and rightly so, because GDP is not a grocery budget. July payroll employment actually fell by 23,000 jobs. May and June were revised downward by another 103,000. Labor-force participation fell to 61.4 percent, its lowest level in five and a half years (read: since Covid). A country can have technically positive GDP, spectacular AI capital spending, record corporate earnings -- and who still have no meaningful cushion for another fifty dollars a week at the grocery store. But of course -- as Project 2025 planned out loud in public -- our current regime in DC demolished to the system America had built to provide that cushion, in the very year it needed to be strongest. The 2025 reconciliation law cuts SNAP by roughly $187 billion through 2034 -- the largest cut in the program's sixty-year history. It raises the work-requirement age from 54 to 64. It hits parents whose youngest child is 14 or older. It strips categorical exemptions from veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth. And the loss of food assistance is already accelerating across the country, reaching older workers nearing retirement age, working parents, and the children in households whose food budgets depend on those adults qualifying for help. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities reports that SNAP participation fell by roughly 5 million people -- about 12 percent -- between July 2025 and May 2026. That decline began before every provision of the reconciliation law was fully in force, so it would be wrong to attribute every lost recipient to the law alone. But the losses accelerated as implementation began, and substantially more people are expected to lose assistance as the remaining provisions phase in. Here in Washington State, DSHS projects the new work requirements will affect 129,000 people statewide, with 73,000 of them losing food benefits outright. The statewide waiver that had exempted much of the state from those requirements ended February 1 of this year. And the state's own share of the bill is about to jump: Washington State's administrative cost share for SNAP rises from 50 to 75 percent this October, with a new state share of actual benefit costs beginning the October after that -- depending on how the state's payment-error rate scores. Then, in September 2025, USDA suspended the Current Population Survey's Food Security Supplement -- the survey that had, every year since 1995, produced the only nationally consistent measure of how many American households can't reliably afford to eat. USDA didn't simply frame this as a budget trim. The agency called the thirty-year survey "costly, politicized," said it amounted to nothing more than "fear monger[ing]," and dismissed three decades of exacting, important, longitudinal data collection as "liberal fodder." Other surveys still exist. The Urban Institute's replacement effort found 24.2 percent of American adults living in food-insecure households in 2025, and its researchers have said plainly that the missing federal data would have helped show exactly how the SNAP cuts are landing as they roll out. But the canonical, thirty-year, congressionally-relied-upon series is gone, cut in the same season the largest SNAP contraction in history began. Put those decisions next to each other and the pattern isn't subtle. DC has slashed the safety net, and stopped measuring the number of people who fall through. We are increasing the number of households exposed to higher food prices at the exact moment we are weakening the institution built to absorb food-price shocks -- and we've already disabled the instrument that would have told us, consistently and nationally, how badly it's going. A drought can reduce a harvest. It cannot decide who goes hungry. People do that. People in power. Markets, wages, SNAP eligibility rules, state cost-share formulas, humanitarian access, and which federal surveys get funded -- those are choices, made by human beings, on a timeline anyone can read. El Niño is natural variability riding on top of a warming planet. Nobody voted for a warming ocean, per se. But nobody made Congress vote to raise the SNAP work-requirement age to 64, either. Nobody made them extend it to parents of fourteen-year-olds. Nobody made USDA call thirty years of hunger data "liberal fodder." Every one of those was a choice, made in public, with a bill number and a roll call attached to it. There are two different hunger stories unfolding on the same timeline. In Sudan, in South Sudan, in the Dry Corridor of Guatemala and Honduras, the question is whether crop failure, conflict, poverty, and shattered humanitarian systems will combine to form famine -- and, whether important, entirely doable choices to preposition seed, cash, and food relief will be made in time. In the United States -- one of the richest, most agriculturally productive societies that has ever existed -- the question is whether we deliberately let people go hungry twenty feet from food they can no longer afford, because we decided, this year, in the thick of increasing climate disruption, to shrink the program that would have caught them and stop measuring how many fell through. None of this requires a miracle to fix. It requires people who already have the maps in front of them to make different choices than the ones they've made so far. Restore the SNAP eligibility rules Congress just narrowed. Restore the national food-security measurement system USDA just abandoned. Treat predictable food-price pressure as something government should prepare households to survive, rather than waiting until food banks are overwhelmed, families are cutting meals, and kids are going hungry -- then calling the result "unfortunate." So, it's on us. Call your state legislators about the October cost-share shift. Call your member of Congress about SNAP and restoring the CPS Food Security Supplement -- the studies that measure hunger in America. Support the food banks in your own county now, before the next round of pressure arrives, not after. The global hunger risk coming through 2027 has already been forecast in public, on a schedule, freely available for anyone to read, by scientists and humanitarian agencies whose job is to warn us before the damage arrives. Here at home, we can already see the conditions that would turn higher food prices into greater hardship: households stretched thin, food assistance contracting, and the country's best historical measure of hunger shut down. We don't know exactly how expensive groceries will get next year. We do know which people the government has decided to leave less protected if they do. I'll keep watching the parts of this that are still moving -- the USDA outlooks, the NOAA updates, the crop reports, the next round of state cost-share numbers -- so you don't have to go dig through them yourself. If that's useful to you, subscribing here is the best way to keep it coming. If you want to help this work go further, I keep a Patreon at . To those who've already provided support, thank you. It means more than you know. [1]Justice Democrats

Peter,

After a flurry of competitive primaries, Justice Democrats is still moving
full steam ahead toward the general election. One of our key races is Mai
Vang for Congress in CA-07.

Mai is a Sacramento City Councilmember running against Do-Nothing Democrat
Doris Matsui — an incumbent and member of a political dynasty who’s been
in Congress for more than 20 years.

This seat is winnable, but only if we build up enough grassroots resources
for Mai to go head-to-head with Matsui’s corporate donors. [ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260830-mv.--mMN9&refcode=em20260830-38215&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=10&t=1002&akid=38215%2E1203867%2EuzlnS9 ]Can you
split $10 between Mai’s campaign and Justice Democrats now
to fuel her fight?

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260830-mv.--mMN9&refcode=em20260830-38215&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=10&t=1021&akid=38215%2E1203867%2EuzlnS9 ]Contribute $10

At a recent debate, Mai showed why she’s the right choice for Congress.

When asked about health care, Matsui flip-flopped and wouldn’t commit to a
direct answer, while Mai stood proudly for Medicare for All.

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260830-mv.--mMN9&refcode=em20260830-38215&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=10&t=1022&akid=38215%2E1203867%2EuzlnS9 ]“Our current health system is broken,” Vang said. “We live in the
richest state and the richest country in the world, yet we can’t provide
health care for our residents.”

Mai also proved herself as the only truly anti-war candidate in this race.
While Matsui is too passive, Mai will vote to stop our tax dollars from
funding genocide overseas and redirect them toward working-class
communities at home.

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260830-mv.--mMN9&refcode=em20260830-38215&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=10&t=1023&akid=38215%2E1203867%2EuzlnS9 ]“We spend trillions of dollars on wars, and what we need to be doing
is spending our tax dollars here, right at home, on systems of care, on
education, on health care,” Vang said.

To transform Congress and the Democratic Party, we need to vote out the
politicians holding us back and replace them with bold, fresh leadership.

The choice in CA-07 is clear: stick with the tired, out-of-touch status
quo or send a fighter for working people and human rights to Washington.

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260830-mv.--mMN9&refcode=em20260830-38215&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=10&t=1024&akid=38215%2E1203867%2EuzlnS9 ]Mai is working hard in these final weeks to win over voters, but she
needs our movement behind her if she’s going to come out on top. Rush a
$10 donation to her campaign and Justice Democrats before
tomorrow’s deadline to help us win!

In solidarity,

Justice Democrats

_You're getting this message because you’ve supported good causes and Democratic candidates. We need your support to continue fighting for our democracy. We love having you in our network, but if you only want our most important email updates,[click here.](https://act.blueampaction.com/go/108?t=2&akid=2959%2E259176%2E5fRbSB) If you'd like to unsubscribe, [click here.](https://act.blueampaction.com/go/109?t=3&akid=2959%2E259176%2E5fRbSB)_

custom_fields.mailing_source_code %}&amount=22) **Major outside groups and billionaire donors are preparing to spend _millions_ in Maine before Election Day.** Here's what that means for us:

body:
Hi there,

It’s Jocelyn Benson. I wasn’t planning on reaching out today, but I just
got off the phone with my fundraising team, and they gave me some bad
news.

Our first end-of-month deadline of the general election is tomorrow at
midnight, and we’re still $5,837 away from our goal.

I’m running against a Trump loyalist who’s funded by millions from the
DeVos family, mega-donors, and shady super PACs. Outside groups have
already spent millions to try to buy this election... and they’re just
getting started.

This is the worst possible time to fall behind.

Some voters are casting their ballots as early as the end of this month,
and we’ve got big plans. We’re knocking doors, hosting events across
Michigan, and have reserved $10 million worth of TV ads.

But we can’t do any of it without this grassroots team by my side.

So while I really hate reaching out and asking for money, I have to ask
before our end-of-month deadline: will you please make your first contribution?
Here’s a link to give: [ https://act.jocelynbenson.com/go/13967?t=1001&akid=1827%2E181023%2EoZoHyC ]secure.actblue.com/donate/benson-email-august26?

Thank you,

Jocelyn
Sent from my iPhone

This email was sent to dpwillis67@gmail.com. Email is a critical way we communicate with supporters like you.
Unsubscribe: https://act.jocelynbenson.com/unsubscribe/unsubscribe-jbmi/?t=1002&akid=1827%2E181023%2EoZoHyC

name: Pramila Jayapal
subject: Why I ran for Congress
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Pramila for Congress
body:
Before I ever ran for office, I was an organizer.
# [](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/892?refcode=em20260830-6663-footer&t=1&akid=6663%2E420207%2ElOSh_m)
Hi Peter, Pramila Jayapal here.
Before I ever ran for office, I was an organizer. After 9/11, when hate crimes against Muslim, Sikh, and South Asian people were spiking across the country, I helped found OneAmerica. We knocked on doors and built power with immigrant families block by block.
I still believe in that kind of organizing. Movements outside of government are how change begins.
But I learned something along the way: Organizing on the outside is even more effective when you _also_ have people organizing on the inside.
**That’s why I ran for Congress.**
I didn’t do it to leave organizing behind, but to bring our work to the inside of a system that too often shuts regular people out.
In the years since I first ran, I’ve worked to build our movement and set the stage for a new generation of bold, progressive leaders like Abdul El-Sayed to run and _win_.
That’s the theory of change I believe in: Outside pressure _and_ inside power get results.
[**So Peter, if you believe, like I do, that we need to organize both inside and outside the halls of power, will you pitch in $3 or anything you can today to help me keep doing both?**](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/47393?c0=pj-em-20260830-1.bEmR56&refcode=em20260830-6663&amount=3&t=2&akid=6663%2E420207%2ElOSh_m)

Pramila Jayapal

name: Beto O'Rourke
subject: Nothing is more powerful than human to human connection
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Powered by People, [poweredxpeople
body:
# [](https://act.betoorourke.com/go/43706?t=1&akid=241043%2E444211%2Ekyd_VP)
There’s suddenly a lot of interest in traditional organizing — essentially, people talking to people without the interference of big money, social media or other technology — in the wake of the upset Democratic primary victories in the last couple of weeks. Reading about how these candidates are getting back to the roots of traditional canvassing reminded me of a moment during my first big race.
We were in the final days of a long-shot bid for Congress and I was knocking on what was probably the 15,998th door of the campaign that we’d launched 8 months earlier. After a minute or two an older woman answered the door, and before I could finish introducing myself (“Hi, my name is Beto O’Rourke, I’m running for Congress and...” ) she invited me in and asked if she could make me a cup of coffee.
I said yes, although I knew that it would probably upset the people I was running the campaign with.
Our whole strategy depended on me personally meeting the voters who were most likely to vote in the election. Because we didn’t have the money for TV (we were outspent 2 to 1) or the name I.D. (the incumbent had been in office for 16 years), we put everything into knocking on doors.
But to get to the target number of voters (somewhere north of 16,000 homes) I had to hit 100-120 a day. That meant spending more than 5-10 minutes with someone would blow up the schedule. I had to be disciplined and get to the goal each day or we weren’t going to make it.
That was always tough for me. The reason I got into politics was because I’m drawn to people. I love getting to know someone, understanding where they’re coming from, figuring out what we have in common. I’m fascinated by the kinds of things you learn, the kind of connection you make, when you’re meeting someone for the first time, especially when you’re meeting them where they are. I’m not saying it always goes well — I’ve had doors slammed in my face, or worse, appealed to people who just couldn’t care less — but when it does, it’s the best thing.
So there was always this tension, between moving quickly enough to meet our targets and moving slowly enough to actually get to know the people I wanted to serve.
When I was at my most focused or when I knew our campaign manager was watching, I could resist the temptation to stay and have a longer talk. But not that day. The offer of hospitality, the kindness being shown to me... the knowledge that air conditioning was on the other side of that door... was too much.
As we walked into the kitchen she showed me a picture of her grandson who’d just enlisted in the Marines. Very proud! His mom, she told me, was a school teacher who did her best to raise her kids right even though she had to take a second job to make ends meet.
The coffee made, we sat down in her living room where she asked me about my family, wanted to know where I came from, who raised me, if I had any kids... you know, the important stuff. Our children were little then, 5, 3 and 1 and of course I showed her pictures and talked about their emerging personalities and our hopes for them.
What struck me about our conversation is that, beyond introducing myself as a candidate for Congress, we didn’t talk politics at all. At the outset I felt an urgency to bring our discussion back to the campaign, but it faded as we fell into the conversation, losing track of time in the process.
But at some point, maybe we’d been talking for an hour or so, I said “Ok, I should probably let you get back to your day and I’ll get back to introducing myself to your neighbors.” I thanked her and gave her a hug at her door and said goodbye. She called out “good luck!” as I walked down the sidewalk to the next house.
I knew that I’d blown our target for the day, but it was nice to just talk to someone, to have a real conversation instead of a transaction, to be a guest in her home, to receive her kindness and encouragement. Not everyone is so nice! She really lifted my spirits that day, gave me a second wind down the final stretch.
The next week, the last one before early voting started, I was walking into a coffee shop when someone stopped me. Asked if I was who I am and after I said yes he said
\- Do you remember knocking on my grandmother’s door? She had you in for coffee... talked your ear off about my brother who joined the Marines...
\- Yes, of course I remember her!
\- Well you must have hit it off, because on Sunday when I and all of my cousins, there’s like 30 of us, came to her house for menudo like we do every week she made us each promise to vote for you. And made us promise that we’d get our friends to vote for you too. I’ve never heard of you before... I wasn’t even planning on voting. But I can tell you now, with our family’s support, you’re going to win this thing.
He was right. On election night we won with a little over 50% of the vote, first in a field of five candidates including the incumbent. I’d go on to win the general election that November.
I knew in my heart that the reason we came out on top was because of all the people I’d met while knocking on doors, all the conversations I’d had, all the time spent just being with the people who were going to vote in this election.
The money, technology, social media, digital ads... all of that’s just substituting for the real thing, human to human connection. Nothing more powerful than that.
That’s why Powered by People organizes by building real relationships and connections. Our volunteers and organizers personally stay in touch with voters and make sure they have everything they need to actually cast their ballot.
[**We can win in 2026, but only if we continue to register and turn out voters across Texas. Can you help support this work by chipping in $3 or whatever makes sense to you today?**](https://act.betoorourke.com/go/56109?c0=pbp-em-20260830.U3L2qZ&refcode=ema20260830-241043&t=3&akid=241043%2E444211%2Ekyd_VP)
Thank you,
Beto

body:
It is well past time to shift the focus from costly vanity projects to the pressing issues facing households across the country.

Last October, I launched my campaign to be the first Democratic Governor of Texas in over thirty years.
Now, we're two months away from Texans casting their ballots, and I wanted to take a moment to recap all that we have built so far to remind everyone what it is we are fighting for: securing the American Dream by saving our public schools and putting money in your pocket.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/c9ae9062-20ec-4e7a-8d8b-203a5ae00972?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Our race has been in the news a lot lately because Texans are ready for change. **We started this race 12 points down from Greg Abbott, closed that gap to 3 points, and now we are effectively tied against Abbott.** That doesn't happen by accident. That's the power of grassroots supporters like you making their voices heard.
I'm humbled by all of the Texans who have invited me into their communities and allowed me to listen to the issues affecting them the most -- data centers in their backyard guzzling up the water and sending electricity costs through the roof, their neighborhood schools closing, selling plasma to make ends meet, and so much more. All the while Abbott has the power to change things and instead chooses to do nothing.
It's time for him to go. In this final stretch of my campaign, I'm going to need your continued support. We have just a few weeks before ballots are cast, and my team and I are driving all across Texas to make sure we win this November. But first...
### **Here 's how it all started:**
Last fall, I announced my campaign to run against Greg Abbott because I knew that Texans deserved a leader who would put them -- not donors -- first. We launched the campaign where I grew up, in the Valley, with a slogan my grandmother taught me: No te dejes. Know your worth and fight for it. I'm ready to fight back.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/b8724ee0-b18b-4825-9af0-bdf62081cb7f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Texans deserve a leader who will fight for everyone to have a chance at achieving the American Dream. Right now, we're all paying the _Greg Abbott Corruption Tax_. Abbott has hoarded $27 billion in taxpayer money - while families struggle to pay their bills. As Governor, I'd issue a $1500 Greg Abbott Corruption Tax refund check to put money in your pocket.
Greg Abbott is out of touch with his base and has been the most unpopular he has ever been. Texans know when they aren't being treated fairly. He has constantly put the needs of his donors before Texans, and we've all had enough.
#### **We launched Team Texas Public Schools.**
Texas Public Schools are in crisis, so we're building a movement for Texans who love their neighborhood schools and are ready to fight for them. It's time we put an end to Abbott's $1 billion school voucher scam.
I remain committed to investing in the education of our kids and retaining quality teachers. We even launched a [toolkit](https://substack.com/redirect/4a5d9e99-824d-460d-acc1-9ce739a62187?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) for parents, teachers, school administrators, and anyone else looking to get involved to amplify our message and help save our Texas neighborhood schools.
I've always believed a quality education is the first step to achieving the American Dream, and that can't happen if schools close or classrooms don't have teachers. I fought against Abbott's voucher scam four times as a state legislator and got my start in advocacy fighting the closure of my own son's local school.
I am beyond ready to keep fighting for Texas kids and undo the damage Abbott has done on our education system.
#### **I went to the soon-to-be largest data center in the world.**
[](https://substack.com/redirect/610d73bf-25dc-44a4-a3f6-e3117b23385f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
I called on Greg Abbott to issue a moratorium on all data centers until our state legislature can meet and put in place real protections for the people of Texas.
Rural communities should not have to compete with mega-corporations for clean water and the right to their land. After years of Greg Abbott opening the floodgates to his data center donors, we need to put a stop to the madness until we can thoughtfully regulate this fast-changing industry.
Abbott can put a stop to data center construction, _today_. Instead, he's haphazardly called for a temporary pause that we all know will evaporate the day after the election. We can't let him get away with it.
### **Here 's how it's going:**
#### **We shattered the attendance record at the Grand Dancehall in Beeville, Texas.**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/15550f10-36df-4b9a-8f99-1f558a0b6149?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I've been visiting deep red towns in Texas and am humbled by all of the support I've received. My race is an opportunity for all Texans to come together and fight back against Greg Abbott's political corruption that has locked working Texans out of key policy decisions.
**I promise you this: help is on the way.**
I'm running to be the leader that Texans deserved in the first place. I won't be beholden to Washington or corporate interests that go against what's best for the people that make up our great state.
Also, shoutout to singer and congressional candidate Bobby Pulido for the amazing concert after our remarks!
#### **Now we 've launched TV ads.**
[](https://substack.com/redirect/3a6155e2-903b-4f96-b93f-c257c8af64fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Texans are hungry for change. When I was a little girl growing up in South Texas, I knew who Texas belonged to. It belonged to all of us. Our beloved state, the land of opportunity, where you could be anything you wanted to be if you worked hard.
I'm fighting hard to get back to that version of Texas. The version that benefits all Texans and not just those at the very top.
